blocks.content: An immutable object is one whose state cannot change after it is created. Once built, it stays exactly as it was for its entire life. This sounds like a small thing but it eliminates entire categories of bugs, makes code dramatically easier to reason about, and is the foundation of safe multithreading.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/55f9b83d-a4ce-496f-a047-ef0ec8dceb4c.png
1. What Does Immutable Mean?
An object is immutable if, from the moment it is created, none of its fields can ever change. You can read from it as many times as you like but you can never modify it.
If you want a "changed" version, you don't modify the original. You create a new object with the updated values and leave the original untouched.

ANALOGY: A PRINTED RECEIPT

When you buy something, the cashier prints a receipt. That receipt is immutable nobody can go back and change the items or price on it. If there's an error, the store issues a new corrected receipt. The original stays as it was. Your receipt is a snapshot of that transaction, frozen in time.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 1. Mutable
A mutable object can be changed after it is created. When you update a value, the original object itself is modified.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/7380fe3b-a496-4592-ae22-bca2416242aa.png
Example: Person name changes from "Alice" to "Bob" in the same object.
2. Immutable
An immutable object cannot be changed after it is created. When you update a value, a new object is created while the original object remains unchanged.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1dfa198a-c051-454b-bb1f-2323890d2c57.png
Example: Original Person still has "Alice", and a new Person object is created with "Bob".
2. Mutable vs Immutable
Let's see both approaches with real code. Same concept a Money value built two ways.
Mutable version (risky)
The cart now contains a price of $0. Nobody told the cart this happened it has no idea the object it holds has been mutated underneath it.
Immutable version (safe)
WHY THIS MATTERS IN PRACTICE

Imagine passing a Money object to a discount service, a tax service, and a reporting service all running concurrently. With a mutable object, each service might be changing the same object at the same time.
With an immutable one, each service gets its own frozen value, reads it safely, and creates a new one if it needs a modified version. No coordination needed. No bugs.
3. How to Build an Immutable (Java)
An immutable class is a class whose objects cannot be changed after they are created. To make a class truly immutable, follow these five rules:
1. Declare the Class final
Making the class final prevents inheritance. Otherwise, a subclass could add mutable fields or override methods and break immutability.
2. Make All Fields private and final
private ensures fields cannot be accessed directly from outside the class, while final ensures they are assigned only once during object creation.
3. Never Provide Setters
A setter's purpose is to modify state. Since immutable objects should never change after creation, setters must not exist.
4. Create Defensive Copies of Mutable Fields
blocks.text: 4. Create Defensive Copies of Mutable Fields

blocks.content: If your class contains mutable objects such as Lists, Arrays, Maps, or Dates, store copies in the constructor and return copies in getters. This prevents external code from modifying the object's internal state.
5. Return New Objects for Updates
Instead of changing the current object, create and return a new object with the updated value. Methods like withName(), withPrice(), or withAddress() follow this pattern.

Note: The concept of immutability is not specific to Java. Most modern languages support it in some form. In C++, immutability is achieved usingconst, private members, and by avoiding setters. In Python, frozen dataclasses and read-only attributes are commonly used. Languages such as Kotlin and C# provide built-in support through data classes and records. Regardless of the language, the core idea remains the same: once an object is created, its state should not change; any update should create a new object instead of modifying the existing one.

blocks.content: 4. The Defensive Copy Rule

This is the rule most developers forget. Even if your fields are private final, if one of them is a mutable object (like a List, Date, or array), someone outside can still mutate your "immutable" class through the reference they passed in or the reference you hand back.
1. The attack from the outside: constructor
blocks.text: 1. The attack from the outside: constructor

blocks.content: BROKEN: THE CALLER MUTATES THE LIST AFTER CONSTRUCTION
FIX: COPY ON THE WAY IN

this.items = List.copyOf(items);  // unmodifiable snapshot taken at construction

// caller's list can change freely — Order is unaffected

// caller's list can change freely — Order is unaffected

codes.javascript:

// caller's list can change freely — Order is unaffected

blocks.content: 2. The attack from the outside: getter
blocks.text: 2. The attack from the outside: getter

blocks.content: BROKEN: GETTER RETURNS THE INTERNAL REFERENCE

List<String> stolen = order.getItems();  // caller gets direct reference

stolen.add("FREE iPhone");               // ← mutates the internal list!
blocks.code:
List<String> stolen = order.getItems();  // caller gets direct reference

stolen.add("FREE iPhone");               // ← mutates the internal list!

codes.javascript:
List<String> stolen = order.getItems();  // caller gets direct reference

stolen.add("FREE iPhone");               // ← mutates the internal list!

blocks.content: FIX: RETURN AN UNMODIFIABLE COPY FROM THE GETTER
1. Defensive Copy on Input
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/cefb765b-3488-4bc2-a80a-f278de319426.png

When a list is passed to an immutable class, List.copyOf() creates a separate copy before storing it. This ensures that changes made to the caller's original list do not affect the object's internal data.
2. Defensive Copy on Output
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/07431a50-18f1-4ea5-9340-c9143fbe7dbf.png

When the list is returned through a getter, List.copyOf() returns a safe copy instead of the actual internal list. This prevents external code from modifying the object's internal state and preserves immutability.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/c07bb4a9-88e5-40e9-b6ed-d77553e24041.png

NOTE ON DATE

java.util.Date is mutable. If your immutable class has a 

Date field, always copy it: this.createdAt = new Date(date.getTime()) on the way in, and return new Date(createdAt.getTime()) from the getter. 

Better yet use java.time.LocalDate or Instant, which are already immutable.

blocks.content: 5. Why Immutability Matters
Immutability is not just style it solves real, concrete problems that mutable state creates.
1. Thread safety for free
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/58c175be-d06a-4dbd-9123-1390d069dc13.png
In a multithreaded system, two threads reading or writing the same mutable object at the same time can corrupt data. You need locks, synchronisation, careful coordination.
With an immutable object, there's nothing to synchronise the object never changes, so two threads reading it simultaneously always get the correct value.
2. Safe sharing across the codebase

You can pass an immutable object anywhere to a method, a thread, a cache, an API response and never worry that the receiver will mutate it out from under you. The object you passed in is the same object when you look at it again later.
3. Easy to cache and reuse

Since immutable objects never change, it's safe to cache them indefinitely. The Java String pool does exactly this identical string literals are stored once and shared, because no caller can mutate the shared copy.
4. Simpler to reason about

When debugging, you never need to ask "who changed this value and when?" An immutable object's value is set at construction and is the same everywhere, for the object's whole life. That's one entire class of bugs that simply doesn't exist.

["No Defensive Programming: With immutable objects, you never have to worry about a caller modifying the data after passing it to your method. Since the object's state cannot change, inputs remain safe and predictable.
","Natural Value Equality: With immutable objects, equality depends on the values stored inside the object rather than its memory location. Two objects containing the same data are naturally considered equal, making comparisons simple and reliable.
","Safe as HashMap Keys: With immutable objects, the hash code remains constant because the object's state never changes. This makes them ideal HashMap keys, eliminating the risk of keys becoming lost after insertion.
","Works Well with Streams and Lambdas: With immutable objects, every transformation creates a new object instead of modifying an existing one. This fits naturally with streams and functional programming, resulting in cleaner and less error-prone code.
"]
items: No Defensive Programming: With immutable objects, you never have to worry about a caller modifying the data after passing it to your method. Since the object's state cannot change, inputs remain safe and predictable.

Natural Value Equality: With immutable objects, equality depends on the values stored inside the object rather than its memory location. Two objects containing the same data are naturally considered equal, making comparisons simple and reliable.

Safe as HashMap Keys: With immutable objects, the hash code remains constant because the object's state never changes. This makes them ideal HashMap keys, eliminating the risk of keys becoming lost after insertion.

Works Well with Streams and Lambdas: With immutable objects, every transformation creates a new object instead of modifying an existing one. This fits naturally with streams and functional programming, resulting in cleaner and less error-prone code.

blocks.content: 6. Immutability in the JDK
Java's standard library is full of immutable classes. Recognising them helps you understand why they work the way they do.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/b552dd55-c3af-48d7-bc9c-3cb2d738d12d.png
String is the best example

codes.python:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    name = "alice"

    upper = name.upper()  # returns NEW string -- "ALICE"

    print(name)   # still "alice" -- completely untouched
    print(upper)  # "ALICE"

blocks.content: Every String method that looks like it "changes" the stringtoUpperCase(),replace(),trim(),substring( actually returns a brand new String.
The original is never touched. This is the immutable pattern in action.

LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15);

LocalDate tomorrow = today.plusDays(1);   // new object

System.out.println(today);               // 2024-01-15 — unchanged

System.out.println(tomorrow);            // 2024-01-16

    print(today)     # 2024-01-15 -- unchanged
    print(tomorrow)   # 2024-01-16

blocks.content: 7. Immutability in System Design (HLD)
Immutability isn't just an OOP concept it shows up at the architecture level too, and for the same reasons: safety, predictability, and no accidental mutation.
1. Immutable messages in event-driven systems

In a system using Kafka, SQS, or any event queue, messages should be immutable events. Once an OrderPlaced event is published, it should never change. Consumers read the event, process it, and publish their own new events. Nobody mutates the original.
ANALOGY: A COURT TRANSCRIPT

In a courtroom, everything said is transcribed and sealed. Nobody can go back and edit what was said. If a correction is needed, a new entry is added: "Witness corrects previous statement." The original is immutable. Event logs work the same way.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/542ecae4-9b47-479e-bf14-193903e6f8fe.png
This diagram shows how immutability is applied to events in a distributed system.

The Order Service creates an order and publishes an OrderPlaced Event. Once this event is published, it becomes a permanent record of what happened at that moment. The event is never edited, updated, or deleted.

Multiple services, such as the Payment Service and Inventory Service, consume the same event independently. Each service reads the event and performs its own work, but none of them can modify the original event.
This approach ensures that the event is published once and read by many services. Since every consumer sees exactly the same data, the system remains consistent and predictable.

If new information needs to be communicated later, the system does not update the existing event. Instead, it publishes a new event (for example, PaymentCompleted or InventoryReserved), preserving the original event forever.
Why This Is Useful

["Consistency: Every service sees the exact same version of the event.
","Auditability: The original event acts as a permanent historical record of what happened.
","Reliability: Services cannot accidentally change data that other services depend on.
","Scalability: Many consumers can process the same event simultaneously without interfering with each other.
"]
items: Consistency: Every service sees the exact same version of the event.
Auditability: The original event acts as a permanent historical record of what happened.
Reliability: Services cannot accidentally change data that other services depend on.
Scalability: Many consumers can process the same event simultaneously without interfering with each other.

blocks.content: 2. Append-only / immutable logs
Event sourcing, audit logs, and database write-ahead logs (WAL) are all built on immutability. Records are only ever appended never modified in place. The log is the source of truth.
Current state is derived by replaying the log. This gives you full history, easy debugging, and safe concurrent reads.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/45cf3fa0-3b2a-4236-8032-c999a8fcc658.png
8. Downsides and When Not to Use It
blocks.text: 8. Downsides and When Not to Use It

blocks.content: Immutability is powerful but not free. There are real costs and real cases where it's the wrong tool.

Object Churn: With immutable objects, every update creates a new object instead of modifying the existing one. For frequently changing data, this can result in thousands of short-lived objects being created, increasing allocation and garbage collection overhead.

Memory Pressure: With large objects that change frequently, creating a new copy for every update can consume significant memory and CPU resources. In such cases, carefully managed mutable state is often more efficient.

Not Ideal for Accumulated State: Some objects are naturally designed to grow over time, such as shopping carts, buffers, or collections that continuously receive new data. Making these immutable can lead to unnecessary object creation and reduced performance.

Not Ideal for Lifecycle-Based Entities: Objects whose state naturally changes throughout their lifetime, such as users, orders, or subscriptions, are often better represented as mutable objects with controlled updates through well-defined methods.
The builder pattern

When you need to construct a complex immutable object step by step (without a massive constructor), use a builder. The builder is mutable while you're assembling the final .build()produces the immutable result.

Java 16+recordtypes give you immutability for free. Declarepublic record Money(String currency, double amount) {}and Java auto-generates a constructor, getters,equals(),hashCode(), andtoString() all immutable by default.
9. Summary
